name: Tocopheryl acetate

card.summary: The stable acetate ester of vitamin E, added to creams and serums as an antioxidant and moisturising ingredient for healthier-looking skin.
card.note: Can cause contact dermatitis in some people; vitamin E acetate in vape liquids was linked to the 2019-20 lung injury outbreak.

quick.overview:
Tocopheryl acetate is vitamin E bound to acetic acid. It is a pale, oily liquid that is far more stable than free vitamin E, which is why it appears in so many moisturisers, sunscreens, serums and supplements.
For skin, it is used as an antioxidant and conditioning ingredient. It can enter the skin and be partly converted into active tocopherol. Reviews have found the evidence for claims such as faster healing or less scarring insufficient, so its role in routines is mainly that of a supporting ingredient in a formula.
quick.how: It is used as a listed ingredient in over-the-counter skincare and make-up, often alongside other antioxidants, and also in oral vitamin E supplements. Most users encounter it rather than buy it alone.
quick.risks: Vitamin E derivatives, including tocopheryl acetate, have occasionally caused allergic contact dermatitis, though the incidence is described as low. Separately, vitamin E acetate used as a thickener in illicit vape cartridges was identified by the FDA and CDC as a strong culprit in the 2019-20 vaping lung injury outbreak; that concerns inhalation, not skin use.

angle.text: It is an ingredient in moisturisers and sunscreens that people use for general skin condition. Its stability is why formulators choose it.

lead: Alpha-tocopheryl acetate, also called vitamin E acetate, is the acetic acid ester of alpha-tocopherol, a form of vitamin E. It is a pale yellow, viscous, fat-soluble liquid that the body can digest back into active vitamin E, and it was first synthesised in 1963 at Hoffmann-La Roche.[1]

In skin care it is one of the most common antioxidant and conditioning ingredients, added to moisturisers, serums, sunscreens and make-up so that skin looks and feels softer and better conditioned. Formulators favour it because blocking the reactive hydroxyl group makes it far more stable than free tocopherol, so it lasts longer in a product and is not notably degraded by air, visible light or UV.[1] It can penetrate skin, and Wikipedia reports that about 5 percent is converted to free tocopherol in living skin cells.[1]

It is also the usual form in vitamin E supplements, and review papers discuss its bioavailability and the potency of natural versus synthetic forms.[2][3][4][9] Two things set it apart in public discussion: marketing claims that it speeds wound healing and reduces scars, which published reviews describe as insufficiently supported, and the 2019-20 vaping lung injury outbreak, in which vitamin E acetate used as a thickener in illicit cartridges was identified as a strong culprit.[1][10]

paras: Tocopheryl acetate has the formula C31H52O3. It is insoluble in water, soluble in acetone, chloroform and diethyl ether and poorly soluble in ethanol, and it does not boil at atmospheric pressure, decomposing from about 240 C.[1] Alpha-tocopherol has three chiral centres, giving eight stereoisomers; the RRR form is the natural one, and the synthetic racemic mixture is called all-rac or DL.[1][2] Hydrolysis, which occurs under suitable conditions or after ingestion, releases alpha-tocopherol and acetic acid.[1]

Vitamin E itself is a family of eight compounds, four tocopherols and four tocotrienols in alpha, beta, gamma and delta forms, with alpha-tocopherol the most biologically active; synthetic supplements are usually the acetate because it is more chemically stable.[9]

Tocopheryl acetate is used in creams, lotions, sunscreens, serums and make-up for its claimed antioxidant effect and as a conditioning, skin-softening ingredient. Its longer shelf life compared with free tocopherol is a main reason it is chosen.[1] A review of vitamin E esters notes that vitamin E has been studied extensively in respect to cosmetic applications as well as disease.[11]

Products and marketing also commonly promote it for wound healing and scar reduction; reviews cited by Wikipedia have concluded that the evidence for those claims is insufficient, and Wikipedia's vitamin E article repeats that reviews have repeatedly found insufficient evidence it aids wound healing or reduces scarring.[1][9]

Vitamin E supplements are usually esterified forms such as acetate, which are hydrolysed and converted into free alpha-tocopherol before absorption in the intestine.[11] In animal tests, natural RRR-alpha-tocopheryl acetate was reported to be 1.36 times more biologically potent than the synthetic all-rac mix, a difference attributed to absorption, transport or metabolism rather than antioxidant activity; a human study using deuterated forms in smokers and non-smokers found natural-to-synthetic bioavailability ratios near 2:1 in earlier competitive-uptake work.[3][4]

In skin, the acetate can penetrate to living cells and is slowly hydrolysed to tocopherol, which may provide some protection against UV; a 1995 rat study is cited in support.[1] Papers on vitamin E stereoisomers and on bioavailability in humans discuss how forms differ in uptake.[2][3][4] A 2024 review notes that vitamin E is commercially used as an antioxidant, though its association with physiological function is described as not linear and its biological roles as multiple.[12]

Herbert McLean Evans and Katharine Scott Bishop discovered vitamin E in 1922 while studying fertility in rats; Evans and Gladys Anderson Emerson isolated it in 1935 and Paul Karrer's team synthesised it in 1938.[9] Alpha-tocopheryl acetate was first synthesised in 1963 at Hoffmann-La Roche, and a 1963 paper in Science reported its biological activity.[1][8] The acetate became the standard stable form for supplements, fortified foods and cosmetics.
Vitamin E derivatives, including tocopheryl acetate, have been linked to allergic contact dermatitis, though incidence is described as low despite widespread use.[1][9]

Vitamin E acetate gained attention in 2019 when US health agencies investigated an outbreak of vaping-associated lung injury. On September 5, 2019 the FDA reported that 10 of 18 vape liquid samples submitted by states tested positive for vitamin E acetate, which illicit THC cartridge makers reportedly used as a thickener; on November 8 the CDC called it a very strong culprit of concern after finding it in lung fluid from all 29 patients tested.[1][10] By early 2020 the CDC had counted 2,758 cases and 64 confirmed deaths, with most cases involving THC-containing products; the agency said other chemicals could not be ruled out, and a 2020 analysis cautioned that vitamin E acetate had not been established as the sole cause.[10][1] A 2020 PNAS study found that vaporising it can produce toxic products including ketene gas.[1] These findings concern inhalation, not skin application.

For oral vitamin E generally, the SELECT trial found that vitamin E did not reduce prostate cancer risk and that longer follow-up showed a statistically significant increase with vitamin E alone; Wikipedia reports a 17 percent higher relative risk.[5][6][9] High-dose supplements may interact with aspirin, warfarin, tamoxifen and cyclosporine A, and the US upper limit for adults is 1,000 mg per day.[9]

Tocopheryl acetate is a routine cosmetic and supplement ingredient. The FDA rejected cardiovascular health claims for vitamin E in 2001 and the European Food Safety Authority rejected similar claims in 2010; in 2016 the US daily value was set at 15 mg as alpha-tocopherol.[9] In the EU, vitamin E is approved as a food additive under E numbers E306 to E309.[9]

No studies have tested topical tocopheryl acetate alone for appearance outcomes in the literature cited here. Oral vitamin E has been studied in large trials such as SELECT, and in smaller trials of conditions such as alcoholic cirrhosis, in which 67 people received 500 mg of vitamin E or placebo daily in a double-blind design.[5][6][7]

lore.intro: Tocopheryl acetate is discussed in skincare and supplement circles mainly as a label ingredient and a form of vitamin E, with claims about scars and anti-ageing that reviews have examined.[1][9]

claims.claim: Vitamin E on the skin heals wounds and fades scars.
claims.believers: Skincare marketing and many users promote vitamin E products for wound healing and scar reduction.[1]
claims.experts: Reviews cited by Wikipedia concluded that evidence for wound-healing and scar-reduction benefits is insufficient.[1][9]

claims.claim: As an antioxidant it protects skin against ageing and UV.
claims.believers: Brands add it as an antioxidant; a rat study suggested released tocopherol may offer some UV protection.[1]
claims.experts: Reviews describe vitamin E's antioxidant role as one of several biological roles and not a linear relationship with function.[12]

claims.claim: Natural vitamin E is better than synthetic.
claims.believers: Natural-form advocates cite the RRR form's higher potency in animal tests, 1.36 times that of all-rac.[3]
claims.experts: The difference is reported to arise from absorption, transport, delivery or metabolism rather than antioxidant activity, and human bioavailability ratios have been debated.[3][4]

claims.claim: Vitamin E acetate is harmless because it is a vitamin.
claims.believers: Because it is a common food and cosmetic ingredient, some users regard it as safe in any form.[1]
claims.experts: The FDA and CDC identified vitamin E acetate as a strong culprit of concern in the 2019-20 vaping lung injury outbreak; vaporising it produces toxic products.[1][10]

claims.claim: Taking high-dose vitamin E supplements protects health.
claims.believers: Observational studies once linked higher intake to lower disease rates, which supported supplement use.[9]
claims.experts: Placebo-controlled trials often failed to confirm this, and SELECT found increased prostate cancer risk with vitamin E alone.[9][6]

claims.claim: Vitamin E in skincare causes rashes for some people.
claims.believers: Some users report irritation or allergic reactions to products containing it.[1]
claims.experts: Allergic contact dermatitis from vitamin E derivatives including tocopheryl acetate is documented but described as uncommon.[1][9]
